Subject: Post-call: Performance SLO qualification & cost/performance levers

Hi Samir / Alex —

Thanks for the time today — good sync. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we’re all aligned: 

Recap of requirements you shared:
- Primary workload: customer-facing chat (streaming responses) integrated into Nova Retail app.
- Latency targets: p95 <= 150ms for streaming tokens; p99 <= 350ms for end-to-end generation (including network).
- Concurrency/throughput: steady-state ~500 concurrent chat sessions; peak bursts up to 1,000 concurrent sessions for holiday promos.
- Typical request size: ~80–140 tokens output, ~25 tokens input.
- Streaming required (chunked tokens to client).
- Accuracy tolerance: small drop acceptable if we can quantify with eval prompts (want to keep >95% of current NLU score).

Action items we agreed:
1) Redwood to propose cost/performance levers (batching, caching, quantization, model variants) and recommended config to meet the SLOs.
2) Redwood to run a short pilot benchmark (your anonymized prompts or our synthetic proxy) on a dedicated pool and share numbers.
3) Schedule a 60-min benching planning call to scope data, success criteria, and timeline.

Attachments: I’ve attached a draft SLO matrix for you to confirm (novaretail-slo-matrix.xlsx). Also attaching our brief on cost levers (redwood-cost-levers.pdf) — Rishi will add more technical detail in his note.

Proposed next steps:
- Rishi to outline specific levers and an initial recommended config (today).
- We schedule the benching planning call — propose Thu 2026-08-07 or Fri 2026-08-08.
- After you confirm, we’ll provision a dedicated pilot pool and run a 24–48 hour workload test.

Samir / Alex — does that match your understanding? Any adjustments to targets or the pilot scope?

Thanks,

Thanks Marissa — that recap looks right. A couple of clarifications from our side before you run the bench: 

1) SLO clarifications:
- p95 <= 150ms target is for streaming token latency (i.e., time from model token emit to client receive). Our product team measures perceived responsiveness by first-stream token; we can provide the exact measurement script.
- For user-facing end-to-end generation across the whole response, we expect p99 <= 350ms as a hard threshold during normal traffic.

2) Load profile:
- Baseline expected steady concurrency 400–600; please size for 500.
- Peak capacity requirement: short bursts (5–10 minutes) of up to 1,000 concurrent sessions during promos.

3) Accuracy / model constraints:
- We’re open to model variants (smaller models) if you can show minimal quality regression on our eval set.
- Please include estimated accuracy delta for quantization approaches (INT8 and INT4) against our eval prompts.

4) Cost target:
- Internal target: keep inference unit economics to no more than 40% increase vs current on-prem costs. We don’t need exact $/token yet — a % delta will help.

Finally, can you confirm whether continuous batching (i.e., batching with a small aggregator window) will add tail latency for single-user sessions? Our UX team is sensitive to anything that increases first-byte latency even by ~20–30ms.

If you can respond with the levers and an initial recommended config + rough cost delta, we’ll lock the benching call date. Thu/Fri next week both work here.

—Samir

Subject: Re: Post-call: Performance SLO qualification & cost/performance levers

Hi Samir — quick technical note on levers and trade-offs. High level first, then recommended pilot config.

Summary of levers (how they affect latency/cost/quality):
- Continuous batching: we use a micro-batching window (1–10ms) to group concurrent in-flight requests; this reduces per-token cost by enabling larger matrix ops but can add a small fixed wait for the first token. For streaming-first-token SLOs, we tune the window low (2–5ms) and enable eager dispatch for single-request outliers; that keeps first-byte impact <~10–20ms in most cases.

- Prefix / KV caching: for repeated prompts or shared system prompts, caching the KV cache can cut work dramatically for multi-turn sessions (p50/p95 improvements). This is high-impact when users have similar context or reused templates.

- Quantization (FP16 -> INT8 / INT4): INT8 typically gives ~2–4x throughput improvement and 30–60% cost reduction vs FP16 on the same GPU, with minimal accuracy impact on many LLMs. INT4 is more aggressive (3–6x throughput) but has a higher risk of regression — we’ll run your eval set to quantify. For Nova Retail, INT8 on a 13B-class model is often a sweet spot.

- Model variants: smaller / distilled variants (e.g., 7B / 13B) reduce latency/cost significantly; 70B gives best quality but higher cost. Our approach: benchmark 13B int8 vs 70B fp16 to measure the quality/cost trade and pick the smallest model that meets your quality bar.

- Dedicated pools + sharding: reserving dedicated nodes for Nova ensures predictable p95/p99 at scale; we can pre-warm KV caches and pin models to avoid cold-start tails.

Recommended pilot config (to target p95 <= 150ms streaming):
- Model: Redwood-13B-int8 (quantized INT8 runtime).
- Deployment: Dedicated pool (2 instance types for headroom), reserved capacity sized for 600 steady concurrent + autoscale for bursts to 1,000 for 10-min windows.
- Continuous batching: micro-batch window 3–5ms with eager dispatch for single-request flows.
- Caching: enable prefix/KV caching for session reuse; warm cache with sampled prompts before peak windows.
- Streaming: chunked token streaming with 1–2 token buffers to the client to minimize perceived latency.

Expected outcomes & rough numbers (approximate, to be validated in pilot):
- Latency: p95 streaming token latency ~80–140ms depending on token size and network; p99 end-to-end ~220–320ms with dedicated pool and cache warm.
- Cost delta: moving from 70B FP16 on shared hosts -> 13B INT8 on dedicated: estimated 3–4x reduction in $/request; compared to a conservative on-prem baseline your finance shared, we expect <40% increase in unit cost (or possibly breakeven) depending on commit/discounts. We’ll provide a CSV with modeled $/token and $/request based on your throughput after the bench.

Caveats / next steps:
- We need a small sample of representative prompts (or let us run a synthetic proxy) to run quantization accuracy checks.
- Pilot bench: 24–48 hours with traffic shape (steady + burst) to validate p95/p99 and cost.
- We’ll produce a one-page bench report and recommend final config for production.

I’ve attached a short cost-levers summary (redwood-cost-levers.pdf) and can share a more detailed cost model once we agree on pilot parameters.

If that looks good, Marissa — shall we lock Thu 2026-08-07 10:00am PT for the bench planning call?

Thanks,
